Title: Science News: Accounting for species’ phenology to estimate population trends from Big Butterfly Count data
Chunks: 0,1
Emily Dennis explains how Butterfly Conservation accounts for species phenology when estimating population trends from the Big Butterfly Count.
Butterfly Conservation’s Big Butterfly Count is one of the world’s biggest nature-based citizen science projects, with over 125,000 people taking part in the UK this summer. The project has been hugely successful in engaging large numbers of observers and raising awareness of the state of the UK’s butterflies, but from a statistical perspective, analysing citizen-science data for biodiversity monitoring can present challenges, such as dealing with various forms of bias 1. In particular, the short three-week sampling period for Big Butterfly Count only captures a small window of species’ flight periods, thus between-year comparisons based on simple metrics are likely to be biased. A recent study2 led by Butterfly Conservation, in collaboration with the University of Kent and UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology, has developed a new approach to account for this phenological bias, and thus enable the reporting of longer-term abundance trends from Big Butterfly Count data for the first time.
Butterfly abundance varies throughout the year as one or more generations of each species emerge and die off, and the timing (phenology) of emergences varies annually due to weather and climate. A previous study 3 based on Big Butterfly Count data from 2011-2014 showed that abundance change estimates for common butterfly species were comparable between Big Butterfly Count and the UK Butterfly Monitoring Scheme (UKBMS) data, however it was also shown that the three-week sampling period rendered Big Butterfly Count “susceptible to bias caused by inter-annual phenological variation in the timing of species’ flight periods”. Thus, there may be the risk of a ‘groundhog effect’ – where a population decline may be falsely indicated by a species’ phenological shift in response to changing climate or other factors 4.

Published in the _Journal of Agricultural, Biological, and Environmental Statistics_, the new study used species’ flight curves estimated from standardised monitoring scheme data (UKBMS), to show that the proportion of the flight period captured by the Big Butterfly Count varies year-to-year for all species, but particularly for summer-flying univoltine (single generation) species, such as Marbled White and Ringlet. For example, the figure below shows how the Big Butterfly Count sampling period (shown in blue) captures different proportions of the Marbled White flight period in four example years, with the proportion varying from 0.12 (in 2011 and 2014) to 0.59 in 2012, when the species peaked comparatively later.
The study adapts a modelling approach that was developed for monitoring data (generalised abundance index 5), drawing upon phenology estimates from UKBMS data, to produce site-level (1km x 1km square) abundance estimates for Big Butterfly Count data that adjust for phenological bias. These phenology-corrected abundance estimates were then combined to produce relative abundance indices and trends for the UK from Big Butterfly Count data for 2011-2022 for 17 common and widespread species.
Comparison to UKBMS trends found that not accounting for phenology leads to biased trend estimates from the Big Butterfly Count data, particularly for the summer-flying univoltine species where the proportion of the flight period captured by the Big Butterfly Count was more variable. The Big Butterfly Count abundance trends were lower than UKBMS trends for 14 out of 17 species, which may be due to the two schemes sampling different habitats: UKBMS transect locations are biased towards sites that are managed for nature conservation, whereas Big Butterfly Count samples more urban habitats, in which butterfly populations have shown stronger declines than in rural areas 6. However, it is also noteworthy that the estimated trends were based on a relatively short period of 12 years which may be sensitive to start year 7 due to the high inter-annual variability in butterfly populations.

## Species-related FAQs
#### Q. Can you help me to identify a butterfly or moth?
Our ID guides are free to download and have been tailored specifically for England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
Download an ID guide
Alternatively, you can visit our identification web pages for help with your identification:
Identify a butterfly
Identify a moth
If after visiting these pages you still cannot identify a species, please contact: [identify@butterfly-conservation.org](mailto:identify@butterfly-conservation.org) with a photo if you have one.

## Species-related FAQs
#### Q. Why isn't every species part of the Count?
Big Butterfly Count is a short snapshot and is aimed to provide a year-to-year comparison for a restricted list of species of butterflies (hence why it takes place at broadly the same time of each year). By restricting the list of species to monitor we minimise counting error and therefore have a clearer view of actual butterfly numbers across the country.
For those species of butterflies and moths which are not on our target species list, you can record them using the iRecord Butterflies App which is available for download on the iOS and Android platforms and has all the butterfly species in the UK.
Other ways to submit sightings of butterflies and moths throughout the year can be found on our website: https://butterfly-conservation.org/butterflies/recording-and-monitoring

## Species-related FAQs
#### Q. Why does the Count only happen during July and August?
The dates of the Big Butterfly Count are carefully chosen to occur at the time when most people will be able to see most butterflies across the whole of the UK.
The impact of the weather can vary year to year, and can impact some regions more than others, but we analyse the scientific data alongside the main flight periods of each species to give us a better understanding of the findings from Big Butterfly Count.
We also compare with data from other butterfly monitoring surveys, such as iRecord Butterflies, the UK Butterfly Monitoring Schemeand the Garden Butterfly Surveywhich take place across the whole year. Meaning that the results of Big Butterfly Count help us to build a detailed picture of how butterflies are faring across the whole of the UK.
* * *

## Count-related FAQs
#### Q. I’ve seen lots of butterflies this year – is there still a Butterfly Emergency?
Butterfly Conservation declared a Butterfly Emergency in September 2024 following an especially bad year for butterflies, and as a result of a long-term decline in butterfly abundance and distribution. 80% of butterfly species in the UK have declined since the 1970s and more than half of butterfly species are now in long-term decline. So, while the numbers of butterflies seen varies from year to year, mainly due to weather fluctuations, the long-term decline in numbers mean that the Butterfly Emergency remains.
* * *

## Technical FAQs
#### Q. Why isn't my app working?
It sounds like you may need to update your app to the latest version.
Android:
1.Open the Google Play Store app Google Play.
2.At the top right, tap the profile icon.
3.Tap Manage apps and device. Apps with an update available are labelled 'Update available'.
4.Tap Update.
Apple / IOS:
1.Open the App Store.
2.Tap your profile icon at the top of the screen.
3.  Scroll to see pending updates and release notes. Tap Update next to an app to only update that app or tap Update All.

## Technical FAQs
#### Q. Why haven't I received my verification email?
Have you checked your spam folder? Most often this is where missing verification emails end up.

## Species-related FAQs
#### Q. Can you help me to identify a butterfly or moth?
Our ID guides are free to download and have been tailored specifically for England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.

## Species-related FAQs
#### Q. Why isn't every species part of the Count?
Big Butterfly Count is a short snapshot and is aimed to provide a year-to-year comparison for a restricted list of species of butterflies (hence why it takes place at broadly the same time of each year). By restricting the list of species to monitor we minimise counting error and therefore have a clearer view of actual butterfly numbers across the country.
For those species of butterflies and moths which are not on our target species list, you can record them using the iRecord Butterflies App which is available for download on the iOS and Android platforms and has all the butterfly species in the UK.

## Species-related FAQs
#### Q. Why does the Count only happen during July and August?
The dates of the Big Butterfly Count are carefully chosen to occur at the time when most people will be able to see most butterflies across the whole of the UK.
The impact of the weather can vary year to year, and can impact some regions more than others, but we analyse the scientific data alongside the main flight periods of each species to give us a better understanding of the findings from Big Butterfly Count.
We also compare with data from other butterfly monitoring surveys, such as iRecord Butterflies, the UK Butterfly Monitoring Schemeand the Garden Butterfly Surveywhich take place across the whole year. Meaning that the results of Big Butterfly Count help us to build a detailed picture of how butterflies are faring across the whole of the UK.
* * *

## Count-related FAQs
#### Q. I’ve seen lots of butterflies this year – is there still a Butterfly Emergency?
Butterfly Conservation declared a Butterfly Emergency in September 2024 following an especially bad year for butterflies, and as a result of a long-term decline in butterfly abundance and distribution. 80% of butterfly species in the UK have declined since the 1970s and more than half of butterfly species are now in long-term decline. ## I'm just seeing a message in the app saying the Big Butterfly Count is now closed
Please update the app by visiting the appropriate app store. This will update the app to the latest version.

## I can't see all of the website
If the website won't open on your browser, try using another one or see if there's a newer version of your browser that you need to download.

## I can't download the ID chart. I opened it and it is blank
If you are having difficulties downloading the ID chart PDF then you may need an updated version of Adobe.

## I can't download the ID chart. I opened it and it is blank
#### Species related FAQs


## Why isn't every species part of the count?
By restricting the list of species to monitor we minimise counting error and therefore have a clearer view of actual butterfly numbers across the country.
If you have spotted species which are not on our target species list here is a handy way you can record them too using the iRecord Butterflies App.

## How can I record a species that isn't part of the count / on the ID chart?
You could download the iRecord app which has all the butterfly species in the UK or go to our website to choose other ways to submit sightings of butterflies and moths.
https://butterfly-conservation.org/butterflies/recording-and-monitoring

## Why aren't males and females of each species shown on the chart?
We have tried to make it as simple as possible for beginners. There isn't space on the ID chart to show all males, females, upper sides and undersides. Most of the butterflies that people see will be males, as they patrol looking for a mate. However, not all of the species on the chart show males – eg a female Meadow Brown is illustrated on the chart.However, in the Big Butterfly Count ID guide there are images of both males and females for species that are noticeably different.

## I don't know what species I have seen - can you identify it for me?
You can identify butterflies here: https://butterfly-conservation.org/butterflies/identify-a-butterfly
You can identify moths here: https://butterfly-conservation.org/butterflies/identify-a-moth

## I don't know what species I have seen - can you identify it for me?
#### Data related FAQs


## What happens to my data?
Full details of how we handle and use your data and butterfly records should be read in our Privacy statement, which you'll agree to when you create an account. In a nutshell, by proceeding to use the website or app to record and submit butterfly sightings you share with us the details of your butterfly observations and also your name, location (collected and defined by your mobile device GPS if using the app) and your email address. Your name and the location (which will be recorded precisely to within metres) of the sighting are important parts of your record and will be included in the butterfly data that we use and share - see Privacy statement for more information about this. Your email address is only shared with individuals responsible for administering this survey or quality checking the data - this will include volunteer County Recorders, see the Privacy statement for more detail.

## Is my count displayed on the map?
A summary of your count, excluding your name, is displayed publicly on the interactive survey map displayed on the Big Butterfly Count website or within the Big Butterfly Count app. The summary appears as a dot on the map at the precise location where you carried out the count. It shows the abundance of each species that you recorded, the date of the count, the number of participants in the count, the habitat type and location name. It does not include your name or email address. You can see local recording results summaries of other contributors by exploring the map. Data are also maintained and shared as part of the scientific record, see FAQ above and Privacy statement.
If you cannot solve your problem here then please get in touch with us at [bigbutterflycount@butterfly-conservation.org](mailto:bigbutterflycount@butterfly-conservation.org)

### **Butterflies bounce back**
Thanks to the many thousands of people who took part in **big butterfly count** 2013 we can see just how well common species fared this summer.
On average, participants saw 23 individual butterflies and moths of the 21 target species per count this year, compared to only 13 individuals per count in 2012.
This massive increase in abundance was reflected across most of the target species and was particularly surprising considering how poor the weather was during previous breeding seasons (whether last summer or this spring). Almost three quarters of species (15 of the 21 target species) showed year on year increases and 12 of them increased by more than 50% compared with 2012.
The ‘whites’ did really well, with Brimstone (380% increase on 2012), Large White (335% up), Small White (312% up) and Green-veined White (214% up) all substantially up on last year.
Although Small White and Large White were the most abundant species recorded, it was Peacock and Small Tortoiseshell that really stole the show for many people this summer. Peacock numbers increased by over 3,500% compared with **big butterfly count** 2012 and Small Tortoiseshells were up by 388%. This is very welcome news for two much-loved butterflies that have declined dramatically in recent years.
Both of the migratory species included in **big butterfly count** also did much better this year compared with 2012. The Painted Lady butterfly and Silver Y moth, both of which undertake long-distance migration into and out of the UK each year, increased substantially (by 380% and 378% respectively).

### **Surprise decreases**
Given the amazing abundance of many butterflies this summer, it was somewhat surprising that any declined compared with the washout summer of 2012. Yet, the species that had done unexpectedly well last year all fell back. Meadow Brown, numbers of which decreased by a third compared to 2012, and in particular Marbled White (59% down) and Ringlet (52% down) suffered substantial year on year declines. Perhaps their larvae suffered reduced survival during the long, cold winter and spring. Six-spot Burnet moth numbers also fell this summer (by 23%).
The **big butterfly count** will return again next summer to enable us to identify longer term trends in our butterfly species. With your help, we can make it even bigger and better in 2014.

The Big Butterfly Count takes place 17 July to 9 August 2026. Read our guide to how you can take part in this important citizen science project, and how to attract more butterflies to your garden
Published: July 16, 2026 at 10:42 am
* * *
Butterflies are an undeniable joy to see in our gardens in summer, fluttering among our flowers and shrubs before resting to feed on sweet nectar in the sunshine.
**Here's the results of the 2025 Big Butterfly Count**
**You may also like**
*   The best plants for butterflies  
*   Boost your butterfly numbers in your garden by doing this one thing  
*   Planting to support butterfly and moth caterpillars  
*   Ten butterflies to identify
While they are a beautiful sight in our gardens, butterflies are among the most threatened groups of wildlife in the UK, with numbers decreasing significantly since the 1970s. This is worrying because butterflies are a vital part of ecosystems, not only as pollinators, but as part of the food chain too.
Butterfly declines are an early warning for other wildlife losses, which is why tracking numbers as part of the Big Butterfly Count will help scientists understand wider changes in the environment and take action for protecting butterflies and other wildlife.
Don't miss our round up of the best plants for butterflies.

## Big Butterfly Count 2026: Everything you need to know
### What is the Big Butterfly Count?
The Big Butterfly Count is a nationwide survey that helps wildlife charity Butterfly Conservation better understand the UK's butterfly population and assess the health of our environment, simply by counting the number and type of butterflies and day-flying moths we see.
The survey first launched in 2010, and last year over 100,000 people took part. The Large white butterfly was the most counted butterfly last year, followed by the Small white and the Gatekeeper.

## Big Butterfly Count 2026: Everything you need to know
### When is the Big Butterfly Count 2026?
This year the survey takes place 17 July to 9 August.

## Big Butterfly Count 2026: Everything you need to know
### Why is the Big Butterfly Count important?
Butterflies and moths are among the most threatened groups of wildlife in the UK, with approximately half of our native species on the red list.
Data from the Big Butterfly Count will help Butterfly Conservation identify important trends in species and assist in their planning for how to protect butterflies from extinction, as well as understanding the effect of climate change on wildlife.
© Andrew Cooper/Butterfly Conservation

## Big Butterfly Count 2026: Everything you need to know
### How do I attract butterflies to my garden?
The best way to attract butterflies to your garden is to plant lots of pollinator-friendly plants that will provide nectar for the butterflies. Pollinator-friendly plants include buddleia, lavender, salvia and _verbena bonariensis_. Butterflies like warmth so try to plant your plants in a sunny, sheltered spot. Read our guide to attracting bees, butterflies and other pollinators to your garden.
Prolong flowering by deadheading flowers, and don't use insecticides and pesticides – they kill butterflies and many pollinating insects as well as ladybirds, ground beetles and spiders.

## I'm just seeing a message in the app saying the Big Butterfly Count is now closed
Please update the app by visiting the appropriate app store. This will update the app to the latest version.

## I can't see all of the website
If the website won't open on your browser, try using another one or see if there's a newer version of your browser that you need to download.

## I can't download the ID chart. I opened it and it is blank
If you are having difficulties downloading the ID chart PDF then you may need an updated version of Adobe.

## I can't download the ID chart. I opened it and it is blank
#### Species related FAQs


## Why isn't every species part of the count?
By restricting the list of species to monitor we minimise counting error and therefore have a clearer view of actual butterfly numbers across the country.
If you have spotted species which are not on our target species list here is a handy way you can record them too using the iRecord Butterflies App.

## How can I record a species that isn't part of the count / on the ID chart?
You could download the iRecord app which has all the butterfly species in the UK or go to our website to choose other ways to submit sightings of butterflies and moths.
https://butterfly-conservation.org/butterflies/recording-and-monitoring

## Why aren't males and females of each species shown on the chart?
We have tried to make it as simple as possible for beginners. There isn't space on the ID chart to show all males, females, upper sides and undersides. Most of the butterflies that people see will be males, as they patrol looking for a mate. However, not all of the species on the chart show males – eg a female Meadow Brown is illustrated on the chart.However, in the Big Butterfly Count ID guide there are images of both males and females for species that are noticeably different.

## I don't know what species I have seen - can you identify it for me?
You can identify butterflies here: https://butterfly-conservation.org/butterflies/identify-a-butterfly
You can identify moths here: https://butterfly-conservation.org/butterflies/identify-a-moth

## I don't know what species I have seen - can you identify it for me?
#### Data related FAQs


## What happens to my data?
Full details of how we handle and use your data and butterfly records should be read in our Privacy statement, which you'll agree to when you create an account. In a nutshell, by proceeding to use the website or app to record and submit butterfly sightings you share with us the details of your butterfly observations and also your name, location (collected and defined by your mobile device GPS if using the app) and your email address. Your name and the location (which will be recorded precisely to within metres) of the sighting are important parts of your record and will be included in the butterfly data that we use and share - see Privacy statement for more information about this. Your email address is only shared with individuals responsible for administering this survey or quality checking the data - this will include volunteer County Recorders, see the Privacy statement for more detail.

## Is my count displayed on the map?
A summary of your count, excluding your name, is displayed publicly on the interactive survey map displayed on the Big Butterfly Count website or within the Big Butterfly Count app. The summary appears as a dot on the map at the precise location where you carried out the count. It shows the abundance of each species that you recorded, the date of the count, the number of participants in the count, the habitat type and location name. It does not include your name or email address. You can see local recording results summaries of other contributors by exploring the map. Data are also maintained and shared as part of the scientific record, see FAQ above and Privacy statement.
If you cannot solve your problem here then please get in touch with us at [bigbutterflycount@butterfly-conservation.org](mailto:bigbutterflycount@butterfly-conservation.org)
